For example, with `max_bytes=1000` and three other snapshot files of 500 bytes each, if process A evicts the oldest file, process B’s first unlink fails, and B then evicts the second file too, leaving only the newest file even though the remaining two would have fit under the cap.

chunk_findings.detail: When `bytes_out > cap` triggers inside the snapshot generation loop, `ValueError("the snapshot is over [log].snapshot_max_mb")` is raised while inside the `fsio.atomic_file(target)` context manager. Because `fsio.atomic_file` relies on file replacement upon clean exit of the context block, raising an unhandled `ValueError` causes the temporary file to be abandoned and deleted, but leaves the caller with an uncaught exception that aborts the read/parse operation entirely rather than falling back gracefully to parsing without a snapshot or respecting the size limit by omitting the write cleanly. This causes any log whose snapshot exceeds `snapshot_max_mb` to crash cold loads with a `ValueError`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new process-global `_SNAP_SWEPT` set is an unbounded memoization cache: each distinct events directory whose disabled snapshots are collected is added as a `Path`, and the only removal point is `_reset_cache`, which is not part of the normal read path (it also clears `_MERGED`/`_SNAPSHOTS` and would therefore defeat the parse caches if called per read). In a long-lived process that reads many different event directories with `[log].snapshot = false`, this set grows without bound, violating [r-bounded-everything]: there is no cap or eviction, so the process retains a `Path` per directory forever.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_parse.py:149 (_SNAP_SWEPT)

chunk_findings.detail: The new max-bytes enforcement counts `mine` in `total` but never adds `mine` to `others`, and only files in `others` are unlinked. If the current snapshot already exceeds `snapshot_max_mb` (for example an existing 300 MB snapshot from before the knob existed, or after lowering `log.snapshot_max_mb` to 50), `_collect_stale_snapshots` leaves `total` over `max_bytes` and the over-cap snapshot survives. The cap is only enforced on newly written snapshots via `_write_snapshot`, not on a pre-existing over-cap current snapshot, violating the `[log].snapshot_max_mb` cap and the cached-data bound.

chunk_findings.detail: The new over-cap branch wraps `mine.unlink()`, `_SNAP_COVERED.pop(...)`, and `total -= mine_size` in one `with contextlib.suppress(OSError)`. If `unlink` raises (for example another process already deleted `mine`, so this process gets `FileNotFoundError`), the `total -= mine_size` line is skipped while `total` still includes the over-cap current file's size. The subsequent loop sees `total > max_bytes` for the rest of the loop and unlinks every file in `others`, even though the current file that caused the overage is already gone. Interleaving: two processes call `_collect_stale_snapshots` on the same log with `max_bytes` below the current snapshot; the first allows the current unlink, the second skips its adjustment and then purges all remaining older snapshots unnecessarily.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_read.py:_collect_stale_snapshots

chunk_findings.detail: The new bound is not atomic. `len(_SNAP_SWEPT) >= _SNAP_SWEPT_MAX`, the later `_SNAP_SWEPT.clear()`, and `_SNAP_SWEPT.add(self.dir)` are separate operations; threads can switch between them. Starting with 255 entries, many distinct-dir readers can all see `< 256`, skip the `clear()`, and then each add its own directory, overshooting the bound by up to the number of concurrent readers. The new regression test is single-threaded and only proves the bound under one execution path, not the claimed hard bounded-cache property.

data.budget: about 40 min, read-only on the real log (copied to scratch), no installs. Not measured: a truly cold disk (the eviction is advisory and only the file pages), and R-scalability's 1.1 GB at 500k was with the fold in the process, which this read_all figure excludes.
data.claim: With the snapshot on, a cold load is slower than parsing the log, on the real log and at 200k to 1M synthetic events, so default-off is right. A parsed event costs 1.4 to 2.5 KB of retained memory, not the 736 bytes the knob doc says, so a 200,000-event ceiling holds about 300 to 500 MB rather than 147 MB.
data.falsifier: Median cold read_all with the snapshot on is below off on the real log, measured in fresh processes with the snapshot verified in use (0 lines parsed, every shard seeded).
data.mechanism: The snapshot does not avoid the expensive work: `_seed_from_snapshot` re-hashes every shard's real bytes (the hash is the trust check) and then unmarshals all objects, which costs more than C json parsing of the same lines, and the frames sit in memory beside the decoded objects, hence the higher peak. The 736-byte figure came from B86's bench, whose events are tiny `task.added` rows; real events carry gate evidence (880 bytes on disk per event here).
data.probe: Scratch scripts one.py/run.sh/seeded.py. Fresh process per run, EventLog.read_all, code at branch head 4e6272fe5, OMP_NUM_THREADS=1. Log: copy of .ddflow/events (137,407 events, 915 files, 121 MB) and logfixture.generate(seed=7) at 200k/500k/1M; separate on and off copies because snapshot=false deletes the files. 7 interleaved off/on pairs for each of 2 cache states: 'keep' (page cache warm) and 'evict' (posix_fadvise DONTNEED on shards and snapshot). Snapshot written by a prior run, snapshot_max_mb raised so it is kept at every size. Memory: tracemalloc retained bytes after gc with the result list dropped, plus RSS from /proc/self/statm in an untraced run. seeded.py wraps _parse_lines and _seed_from_snapshot. R-scalability read in full first: its finding 3 is the same claim at 132k.

data.question: Is a cold load with the marshal read snapshot on slower than with it off on a real-sized log, and what does a parsed event really cost in memory?

chunk_findings.detail: `_discard_disabled_snapshots` gates the cleanup on `self.log_cfg.snapshot`, but the effective setting is `_snapshot_enabled()`: `SNAPSHOT_ENV` can switch snapshots on per process even when `[log].snapshot` is false (the new default). In that situation the branch still deletes every `read-snapshot*.bin` before the read that the environment switch is explicitly enabling, destroying the cache this run was meant to use. The docstring says “The per-process environment switch never does” this sweep, but the code does not consult `_snapshot_enabled()` or `SNAPSHOT_ENV`, so it does exactly the documented no-no.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_read.py:_discard_disabled_snapshots

chunk_findings.detail: The note tells users "Set log.snapshot = true to keep it; old snapshot files stay readable when it is on", but the new `log.snapshot_max_mb` cap added by the same change explicitly deletes "the oldest snapshots of other versions" when the cap is exceeded. So with `log.snapshot = true` and over 256 MB of old snapshots from other versions, old snapshot files do not stay readable/retained as promised.
